This browser can't connect to USB sticks. OFFgrid-SDR uses WebUSB, which works in Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge and other Chromium-based browsers (Opera, Vivaldi, Chromium). Firefox and Safari don't support it. You can still try everything without a stick in demo mode.

Receiver settings

Saved automatically on this computer

Device

Halves the samples the stick sends (1.024 MS/s, a narrower view) and draws the spectrum and waterfall half as often. Everything else keeps working. Off by default.
HF upconverter (Nooelec Ham It Up and others)
With a converter in front of the stick, 5 MHz arrives at the stick on 130 MHz: this keeps every frequency shown the real one. Auto uses it below 65 MHz (MW, shortwave, HF) and tunes straight through above (FM, airband, VHF); its switch is a physical one, so OFFgrid-SDR reminds you which way to set it. The oscillator is 125 MHz on current Ham It Ups (100 MHz on older ones; 120 MHz on a SpyVerter). SDR# and SDR++ call this a frequency shift of −125 MHz: it's the same thing, and either can be typed here. A standard one can be a few kHz out: Frequency calibration on a time station corrects the stick and the converter together.
Bias-tee (antenna power) With an SDRplay RSP, OFFgrid-SDR can't switch the bias-tee or see it: SDRconnect's WebSocket API (1.0.3) has no bias-tee control. For a powered antenna, use its own bias-tee injector, or SDRconnect's ordinary program with the bias-tee on. For LNAs and active antennas made to be powered this way (RTL-SDR Blog V3 and V4: 4.5 V). Leave it off otherwise: some antennas short DC to ground, and powering them can damage the stick or the antenna. The red BIAS light shows when it's on.
DC spike Removes the stick's constant offset, which shows as a spike in the middle of the MW and SW views.

Display & tuning

Signal info popup Centre frequency, level, how far above the noise, width, the band plan and your own labels. Off by default: it only works while you move the mouse, but it is one more thing to run on a slow PC. Touch screens have no hover, so it doesn't show there.

Audio & recording

Peak limiter It only acts if what's coming out of your speakers or headphones would reach full scale, so at normal volume it leaves the programme alone.

Decoders

RDS (FM) RDS needs a better signal than the audio does. On a weaker station the name may take a few seconds to build up (missing letters show as dots). If RDS drops out, the last name and text stay on screen, dimmed.
FT8 and FT4 decoding After decoding, the stations found are taken out of the signal and it decodes again, up to three times, as WSJT-X does. Stations it finds that way are marked ◆ in the list, and the header counts them. Turn it off to compare with the plain decoder on the same band (the counts start again each time you switch).
FM band for your country
FT8 and FT4: your station Your callsign highlights anyone calling you in the list; your location gives the distance and bearing to each station. Pick your nearest city (620 are built in, so this works offline), type your locator, or ask the computer (that only works with a GPS, or with the internet for Wi-Fi positioning). Kept on this computer only. The country of each station comes from its callsign, using a table built into the app: nothing is looked up online.
CW decoder Shown bottom left in CW mode. Best on clean, steady signals such as beacons; it learns the speed by itself. The first letter or so of a transmission may be missed while it locks on.
Weather fax Each finished chart is saved as a PNG to your Downloads folder, so none are missed while you're away. (Even with this off, a chart isn't lost if the next one starts before you save it: use "Save previous" in the fax box.) Chrome may ask once to allow several downloads: choose Allow.

Calibration

Frequency calibration
Pick a time station and press Calibrate: it tunes there, measures the carrier and sets the correction above. Best done after the stick has been running for 10–15 minutes.
Setup and clock
The setup sets your location, calibrates the stick and sets the clock from a time station, in one go. Clock details shows how far your computer's clock is out, how fast it drifts, and how to set it.
S-meter calibration
dBm
Tune to a signal of known strength (a signal generator, or a beacon with a known level), set manual RF gain, type its level and press Calibrate. HF and VHF are stored separately. The S-meter needs manual gain, because AGC hides the real gain.

Backup

Settings backup
Saves all 50 memories, each band's last frequency and mode, filters, calibration and other settings to a small file, for example to keep on the USB stick with OFFgrid-SDR, or to copy them to another computer. Importing replaces the current settings.
Diagnostics
If the spectrum or waterfall stops, save this straight away and send it with your report. It holds the last three minutes of band changes, retunes, sample-rate changes and timing (no audio, no memories, no personal details).

Click the frequency display to type a new frequency. Waterfall: click anywhere to tune there (a signal is tuned exactly), or click close to the tuning line to step one channel. Shift-click tunes to the exact spot. The mouse wheel steps one channel per notch. Keys: ← → step, Shift + ← → seek, M mute. Seek stops on the first channel whose S/N is above the squelch level. With squelch fully open, it stops at 10 dB S/N. MW and the SW metre bands are shown whole: the stick parks on the middle of the band and tuning moves only the demodulator. Fully self-contained: runs offline, no internet needed. Try index.html?demo for simulated stations without a stick. Needs Chrome, Edge or Opera with WebUSB. For MW and SW, use a long wire or HF antenna.

Welcome to OFFgrid-SDR

FT8, FT4 and WSPR work best with the right time and a corrected stick: a few minutes, only needed once, and you can skip any part
  1. Location
  2. RTL stick and clock
  3. Results

This setup tells OFFgrid-SDR where you are, corrects your stick's frequency (some sticks are tens of ppm out) and sets an accurate clock from a shortwave time station, with no internet needed. FT8, FT4 and WSPR only decode when the clock is right to within a second or two. If your computer is online its clock is probably fine already, and you can skip all of this. The stick can also be calibrated at any time with the Calibrate button in Settings → Calibration.

You can skip any step, or the whole setup. OFFgrid-SDR then uses your computer's own clock as it is (FT8 still fine-tunes the seconds from the stations it hears) and the stick without a correction. You can run this again any time: Settings → Calibration → Run setup again.

Where are you? This gives the distance and direction to the stations you hear, sets the FM band for your country (it is 76–95 MHz in Japan, for example), and helps choose time stations for the time of day. It stays on this computer.

OFFgrid-SDR will look for a shortwave time station (CHU, WWV or RWM). Its carrier is on an exact frequency, so it calibrates your stick; its time code sets the clock. It tries the likeliest stations for the time of day first, and takes about 2 to 4 minutes, up to 7 if they are hard to hear. Have the antenna connected.

Can't hear a station, or just want to set the clock now? Set the time by hand, for example from a phone: type the UTC time a few seconds ahead, and press Set when the phone shows it. (This sets the clock only; the stick is calibrated by a time station, or later with the Calibrate button in Settings → Calibration.)

UTC

Skipping this step leaves the clock as the computer has it and the stick uncorrected. You can do it later from the Time signal mode, or run the setup again.

Switch the radio on first: 


      
No time station could be heard just now (they come and go with the time of day). You can try again later, or set the time by hand above.

        
The stick doesn't need a time station to be calibrated: WSPR works from the stations themselves. Set the clock by hand first, then . Settings → Calibration also has a Calibrate button.

    

    

      
The stick has not been calibrated. No time station is needed: with the clock set, WSPR can do it from the stations it hears (10 to 20 minutes on 20 m).

New in 2.3

    
    
      
  • SDRplay RSPs, through SDRconnect (requested feature): OFFgrid-SDR can use an RSP on SDRconnect (1.0.6 or later, with its WebSocket API switched on; on a computer without a screen, SDRconnect's headless program, not "--server"), on another computer on your network or this one (127.0.0.1). Choose it when you first open OFFgrid-SDR ("Select device to connect to"), or in Settings → Device: enter the PC name or IP address, press Test, then Power on. The last 5 addresses that worked are offered; the RF gain slider sets the RSP's front-end (LNA) gain, higher for more as usual, with full gain only in its last tenth (it overloads easily), and Auto picks the middle setting for each band (the IF gain is left to SDRconnect's AGC); OVL shows SDRconnect's own overload; a lost connection is retried by itself. An RSP with several antennas (RSPdx, RSPduo) switches them by frequency: by default A from 30 MHz up, B below, C not used, each changeable (including a custom range); an RSPduo uses one tuner. The bias-tee can't be controlled from OFFgrid-SDR: SDRconnect's WebSocket API (version 1.0.3, in SDRconnect 1.0.10) has no bias-tee control, and its headless program no bias-tee option. For a powered antenna (an active loop such as the MLA-30+, say), use the antenna's own bias-tee injector, or SDRconnect's ordinary program with the bias-tee switched on. (An optional SDRconnect profile can be applied when connecting, for other settings.) Panorama isn't available through SDRconnect (it sweeps faster than a network connection can follow). It needs no USB, so it works in any browser; the stream needs about 8 MB/s, so a wired link or good Wi-Fi. The full guide is SDRconnect.md, beside the README on GitHub.
    • 
      
  • What you're listening with, before the band name: RTL (a USB stick), NET (SDRconnect: green keeping up, amber connecting or falling behind, red lost) or DEMO. Hover over it, or tap it, for the details: for NET, the network speed against what's needed, the buffer, gaps, the device and its settings.
    • 
      
  • Plain messages when the stick can't tune, including when the HF upconverter setting is switched on without an upconverter fitted.
    • 
      
  • Resting when switched off: the display no longer redraws 60 times a second while the radio is off (it's woken by the mouse, touch or keyboard), and the waterfall stays still, its time marks too.
    • 
      
  • Journaline news pages on DRM: when a station sends them (All India Radio does), a News button appears in the DRM box: menus, articles and lists, kept as they arrive. The demo's 11.700 MHz station has a few to try.
    • 
      
  • DRM through fades: a fade no longer stops the sound to rebuffer: it's bridged silently and comes straight back (faded in). Frames in a fade are decoded a second and third time, the layers helping one another: on a fading recording of TDF on 5.990 MHz, 36% fewer dropouts. And a drifting signal (an upconverter warming up) is followed through each window.
    • 
      
  • Sharper DAB logos on high-resolution screens (the stored large logo, scaled down).
    • 
      
  • The screen stays on while the radio is powered on (for tablets used as a radio); it's released when you power off.
    • 
      
  • A lighter noise blanker: 40% less work, exactly the same result.
    • 
      
  • The noise blanker and hum filter in CW and the digital modes (FT8, FT4, WSPR, RTTY and the rest) on MW and SW: switching from USB to FT8 no longer brings the clicks and hum back. Noise reduction, the notch and the AI cleaner stay with voice.
    • 
      
  • A clean DAB waterfall: no more dark lines across it every few seconds (each line now spans more than DAB's short null symbol).
    • 
      
  • Backups checked as they're loaded: a damaged or tampered backup can no longer upset the page; anything malformed is simply left out.
    • 
    

    
New in 2.2

    
    
      
  • Five band tabs: FM · DAB · MW · SW · Air. DAB and Airband have their own tabs (each opens your last channel there); SW keeps Broadcast, Ham and Mystery, and always returns to your last shortwave frequency. On a narrow panel the tabs wrap onto two rows.
    • 
      
  • DAB station text: "now playing" and programme information under the station's details, with its programme type (News, Pop Music and so on).
    • 
      
  • DAB station logos from the multiplex's picture service (as the BBC sends them), top right of the DAB box; click for the large one. They're kept, so they appear at once on later visits; a first visit collects them over a few minutes, whichever station is playing. Hover over the multiplex's name to see how many have arrived, or whether the multiplex sends any at all.
    • 
      
  • DAB SlideShow: pictures a station sends with its sound (common in mainland Europe) show in the logo's place: the latest one if the station has no logo, or each new one for 10 seconds before the logo returns.
    • 
      
  • DRM station text and pictures: the station's text message under its details, and its SlideShow picture top right.
    • 
      
  • More DAB stations play: MP2 stations at 24 kHz (Times Radio, Fix Radio and others), joint-stereo MP2 from encoders that switch modes, the highest MP2 bit rates (320 and 384 kbit/s), and every protection level, checked against every combination the standard allows. Accented station names show correctly.
    • 
      
  • DAB fixes: a DAB+ station could go silent until retuned; the receiver now re-locks by itself if its lock goes stale, rides through brief dips, and no longer applies the audio filters (as DRM). The waterfall's regular dip on DAB is gone.
    • 
      
  • Faster, for slower computers: DAB and DRM decode with much less work, the display no longer makes the browser redo its layout every frame, and hovering over the CPU figure shows where the time goes. On a five-year-old Chromebook, DAB+ fell from about 60% to under 50% of a core, and AM from 38% to 24%.
    • 
      
  • VDL2 (requested on GitHub), under More → Aircraft beside ACARS: aircraft datalink at 136.6–137 MHz, every channel in view decoded at once (from your locator: in Europe 136.675, 136.725, 136.775, 136.825, 136.875 and 136.975 MHz). ACARS messages in full, the rest summarised; each aircraft's country from its address (built in, offline); channel buttons with counts to filter the list, and "Messages only" to hide acknowledgements. AUTO knows the channels too.
    • 
      
  • Full screen / kiosk mode (requested on GitHub): the button at the right of the top bar, or the F key.
    • 
      
  • The More menu, grouped: Voice, Digital radio, Aircraft, Ships, Ham digital, Pictures and Time signals.
    • 
      
  • Selecting further back in the paused waterfall: drag a box towards the bottom edge and the waterfall scrolls back in time by itself (towards the top, forwards); the box stays with the signal as it scrolls. ↑ and ↓ move through the paused history, and a scroll bar on the right shows where you are.
    • 
      
  • 108–118 MHz (aircraft navigation: VOR and ILS beacons) now opens in AM, in 50 kHz steps.
    • 
      
  • In the demo: station text, logos and a SlideShow on "OFFgrid DAB" (12A), text and the OFFgrid-SDR logo on both DRM stations (11.700 and 11.750 MHz), and VDL2 aircraft on 136.975, 136.775 and 136.675 MHz.

New in 2.1

    
    
      
  • DAB and DAB+ digital radio, with sound: choose a channel in the band chips' new DAB group (5A to 13F), or tune anywhere in a multiplex with AUTO on. The box bottom left shows the multiplex's name and its stations: click one to listen. Both kinds play: DAB+ (HE-AAC, through FAAD2) and the original DAB (MP2), still used by many stations, the BBC's among them.

New in 2.0

    
    
      
  • DRM digital radio, with sound (More, or AUTO). Tune to the centre of a DRM station (a flat block about 10 kHz wide on long, medium or short wave) and the DRM box shows the station's name, language and audio type, then plays its sound (AAC, including SBR and parametric stereo), about 5 seconds behind the signal as on any DRM receiver. It finds the station's robustness mode (A to D) and bandwidth by itself, copes with tuning a few hundred hertz off centre, reads signals that arrive mirrored, and leans on the cleaner carriers when part of the channel has interference. Tested on real broadcasts in modes A, B and C, mono, SBR and parametric stereo: every one plays.
    • 
      
  • When a DRM station can't be played, the box says why, with its name and settings still shown: the xHE-AAC audio codec, two protection levels (unequal error protection) or hierarchical modulation, which OFFgrid-SDR can't decode yet, or a data service without audio.
    • 
      
  • DRM signal quality in the DRM box (in dB), and a plain explanation when a signal is too weak for its name and sound: 16-QAM stations need about 10 dB, 64-QAM about 16.
    • 
      
  • AUTO recognises DRM and switches to it, centred on the station. If it ever takes an AM station for DRM (it can happen, now and then, on a heavily loaded computer), the DRM reader finds no DRM signal there within a few seconds and it goes back to AM by itself.
    • 
      
  • The waterfall replay reads DRM: pause, draw a box around a DRM signal (about 4 seconds or more) and the replay window shows the station's name and settings. The sound replays as it sounds on an ordinary receiver; the digital sound plays live only.
    • 
      
  • The demo has a real DRM station: "OFFgrid DRM" on 6.095 MHz, playing an original jingle, so anyone can try DRM, and see whether their computer keeps up, without a DRM station in range.
    • 
      
  • 6 m and 4 m in the Ham bands, between 10 m and 2 m, in USB. Their edges follow where you are: 6 m is 50–52 MHz in Europe, Africa and the Middle East and 50–54 MHz in the Americas and Asia-Pacific; 4 m is 70.0–70.5 MHz in the UK and 69.9–70.5 MHz elsewhere in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, and isn't shown where there's no 4 m band (the Americas and Asia-Pacific).
    • 
      
  • A wider status line: the messages now have the top bar's whole line to themselves (on a 1366-pixel laptop, over five times the room), with the CPU and FPS figures on a smaller line beneath.
    • 
      
  • A fuller CPU figure, and no RAM figure: CPU now includes the decoders working in the background (DRM, FT8), so it can show over 100% (more than one processor core's worth): hover over it for the split. The RAM figure is gone: a web page can see well under half of the memory it really uses (not the browser's own share for it, nor its background decoders'), so the figure was misleading. Chrome's Task Manager (Shift+Esc) shows the real figure for the tab.
    • 
      
  • OFFgrid-SDR is now free software under the GNU GPL, version 3 or later (see the credits below).
    • 
      
  • Fixed: the waterfall replay of DRM, AIS and APRS. Pausing and drawing a box around one of these left the replay window on "Preparing…" for good: the replay didn't know how to play those modes. They now replay (DRM as AM, AIS and APRS as narrowband FM), and if a selection ever can't be prepared, the window says why instead of waiting forever.
    • 
      
  • Fixed: reopening the replay window briefly showed the previous selection's details.
    • 
      
  • Fixed: noise reduction could do little for many seconds after a brief gap in the audio (a busy computer, a retune): it took the moment of silence for the noise level. It now ignores gaps: measured, the reduction stays at about 8 dB after one, where it fell below 2 dB before.
    • 
      
  • Fixed: RTTY's automatic reverse could leave a station the wrong way round (mark and space swapped, the text gibberish) for a minute or more, when its text read only a little better the right way. It now also compares the last hundred or so characters, so a steady difference is caught: on the demo, every test case came back the right way within half a minute, where before most didn't within 45 seconds.
    •

New in 1.9

    
Setup and the clock

    
    
      
  • Setup for FT8, FT4 and WSPR: the first time you choose FT8, FT4, WSPR or Time signal, a short setup offers to set your location (asking the computer's own location straight away, with a list of cities as well), find a shortwave time station, whose carrier calibrates your stick and whose time code sets the clock, and show the results. You can skip it, or set the time by hand if no station can be heard. Other modes never ask. Run it again any time from Settings → Calibration → Run setup again.
    • 
      
  • Clock details: how far your computer's clock is from the time stations, how fast it drifts, the correction in use, and how to set the computer's own clock. From the Time signal box or Settings → Calibration.
    • 
      
  • A smarter clock: two time-signal readings a day or more apart teach OFFgrid-SDR how fast your computer's clock drifts, and it follows that between checks. If the last check is getting old, it says so. When the computer is online, an old correction is dropped, as the internet has probably set its clock.
    • 
      
  • Find a time station no longer wastes time on an empty frequency, tries the stations that give the time quickest first, and copes better with a stick that's well off frequency.
    • 
      
  • Fixed: after a restart, OFFgrid-SDR forgot where its clock correction had come from.
    • 
    

    
WSPR

    
    
      
  • Decodes even with the clock well out: WSPR now keeps the last four minutes of audio and searches two whole minutes of start times, so its stations are found with the clock up to a minute or so out. Their timing then puts the clock right to within a tenth of a second, which FT8 alone can't do beyond 7.5 seconds: a computer that's been away from the internet for weeks comes right just by listening to WSPR.
    • 
    

    
New mode: APRS

    
    
      
  • APRS (More): radio amateurs' positions, weather stations, messages and status reports on VHF, decoded from their 1200-baud data bursts and listed like FT8: each station with its distance and bearing, speed and heading, height for balloons, and weather in °C, km/h and hPa. Choosing APRS goes to the frequency for where you are (144.800 MHz in Europe, 144.390 in North America, 145.175 in Australia; the list in the box has the others, and the International Space Station's). Only error-free packets are shown, and a packet repeated by digipeaters appears once. The demo has an APRS station on 144.800 MHz.
    • 
    

    
New mode: AIS (ships)

    
    
      
  • AIS (More): ships' automatic identification, decoded on both marine channels at once (161.975 and 162.025 MHz). Each vessel appears once, updated as it's heard: its name, type, distance and bearing, speed and course, whether it's at anchor or moored, and where it's bound; hover for its MMSI, flag, call sign, size, draught and ETA. Coast stations and buoys too. Only error-free messages are shown. The demo has ships in Liverpool Bay.
    • 
    

    
HF upconverters

    
    
      
  • Ham It Up and other HF upconverters: Settings → Device → HF upconverter. With one in front of the stick, a station on 5 MHz arrives at the stick on 130 MHz; this keeps every frequency shown the real one. Auto uses the converter below 65 MHz (MW, shortwave, HF) and tunes straight through above (FM, airband, VHF), reminding you which way to set its switch; On uses it always. Off by default. The oscillator is 125 MHz (100 MHz on older Ham It Ups, 120 MHz on a SpyVerter), with fine tuning in Hz; Frequency calibration on a time station corrects the stick and the converter together.
    • 
    

    
Smaller changes

    
    
      
  • The FM band for your country: chosen from your location: 87.5–108 MHz for most of the world, 87.9–107.9 MHz on a 200 kHz raster in the USA, Canada and Mexico (stepping 87.9, 88.1, 88.3…), 76–95 MHz in Japan, 76–108 MHz in Brazil and Chile, and 65.8–108 MHz with the old OIRT band in Russia and some former Soviet republics. Settings → Decoders, beside your location, can override it.
    • 
      
  • Memories are safe while a backup is being imported: they're kept in memory for the moment, and the ones saved in the browser aren't touched until the import is done.
    • 
      
  • Each stick keeps its own frequency correction: plug a calibrated stick in again and its correction comes back; a different stick starts at 0 ppm rather than inheriting one that isn't its own. (Sticks with the same serial number can't be told apart.)
    • 
      
  • AUTO no longer takes a broadcast station deep in a fade for Hellschreiber: Hell is only looked for in the amateur bands, where it's sent.
    • 
      
  • Demo, fixed: going from the airband or VHF back to shortwave could stop the demo's samples, and after 3 seconds the radio switched itself off (its timing wasn't re-anchored when the sample rate fell from 2.4 to 2.048 MHz, so it waited tens of seconds to catch up; it depended on timing, so some computers met it every time).
    • 
      
  • Demo, fixed: on a busy computer the demo could freeze OFFgrid-SDR (its signals are made on the same thread as the page, and catching up took all of it). It now lightens itself instead, leaving out distant stations, or for a while everything but background noise.
    • 
      
  • Demo, fixed: on the airband and VHF, the demo's background noise had a 14 ms break every half second (its noise table was shorter than a batch of samples at 2.4 MHz). Voice and ACARS hid it; APRS packets couldn't.
    • 
      
  • Demo: the 40 m and 41 m bands run more than twice as fast, so the time stations' codes and the other decoders keep up on slower computers.
    • 
    

    
New in 1.8

    
New modes

    
    
      
  • WSPR (More): radio amateurs' weak beacons, decoded every 2 minutes down to about −28 dB, far below what you can hear. They show in the FT8 list with callsign, country, distance, bearing and transmitter power (dBm and watts), with a band list from 2200 m to 2 m. If the stations land away from where they should, the box shows how far off your stick is, and Correct fixes it.
    • 
      
  • Time signal (More): sets OFFgrid-SDR's clock from the shortwave time stations, with no internet, even if the computer's clock is hours out. CHU (Canada) gives the full time in about 15 seconds, WWV and WWVH (USA) at the end of a minute, RWM (Russia) the exact second. Find a time station tries them all; a weak station's ticks still set the seconds; if none can be heard, Set by hand takes the time from a phone. The box always shows where the clock came from.
    • 
    

    
FT8 and FT4

    
    
      
  • Deeper decoding: the stations found are rebuilt and taken out of the signal, and it decodes again, up to three times, so weaker stations hidden under strong ones come through (as WSJT-X does). They're marked ◆, the box's header counts them, and a switch in Settings → Decoders turns it off to compare. It adapts to the computer, using fewer passes if decoding runs long.
    • 
      
  • Band lists: at the top of the box, straight to the FT8 or FT4 frequency on any band.
    • 
      
  • Room for uncalibrated sticks: FT8, FT4 and WSPR listen from 1.5 kHz below the dial to 4.5 kHz above it, so a stick that's off frequency either way keeps the stations in view.
    • 
      
  • A tidier list: the columns line up with their headings, the scroll bar no longer covers the bearings, and the header stays on one line.
    • 
    

    
Propagation

    
    
      
  • Heard: who can your station hear? The Heard button in the FT8 box sums up the last 15 minutes, hour or 3 hours band by band: stations, countries, the farthest, which directions the band is open towards, and whether it's rising or fading. Click a band for its countries and a compass. Built from every FT8, FT4 and WSPR decode, and kept when you clear the list.
    • 
      
  • Band survey: under Heard, Survey bands listens to the FT8 frequency on each band from 80 to 10 m in turn (about 5 minutes), then comes back, so you can see at a glance which bands are open.
    • 
    

    
The stick

    
    
      
  • Radio library updated to webrtlsdr 3.0.7 / signals 0.10.2 by Jacobo Tarrío, with the fixes found with OFFgrid-SDR built in: the RF gain is no longer lost when you switch off and on (the cause of weak reception after a restart on some computers), no frequency drift after a restart, a stick that stops sending no longer hangs the radio, and a firmer tuner lock. OFFgrid-SDR no longer needs its own patched copy.
    • 
      
  • Power pressed while switching (off and straight back on) is remembered and done, rather than lost.
    • 
      
  • The OVL back-off works with the window in the background too.
    • 
    

    
Smaller changes

    
    
      
  • The clock at the top shows the corrected time, once a time station or FT8 has set it.
    • 
      
  • FAX, ACARS, WSPR and Time signal can be chosen from the FM band: they go straight to a station.
    • 
      
  • Audio extensions (equalisers and the like): a note in Quick help on allowing them when OFFgrid-SDR is opened as a file.
    • 
    

    
Demo

    
    
      
  • New stations: WSPR on 14.0956 MHz, CHU on 7.850 MHz, WWV on 10 MHz, RWM on 4.996 MHz, and a weak FT8 station on 14.074 MHz (EI2OGS) hidden under K1OGS, which only the deeper decoding finds.
    • 
      
  • More realistic: the FT8 and FT4 stations are shaped like real transmitters' signals, and the busiest bands run several times faster, so the demo keeps up on slower computers.
    • 
    

    
New in 1.7

    
AUTO

    
    
      
  • SSB, found and tuned for you: AUTO finds an SSB voice wherever the dial sits on it (even faint ones), picks the sideband, and tunes to the carrier to within a few Hz by lining up the harmonics of the speaker's voice, so voices sound natural without fine-tuning.
    • 
      
  • More modes recognised: FT8 (on the FT8 frequencies), ACARS (on its channels), PSK63 and PSK125 as well as PSK31, and DRM tuned to its centre.
    • 
      
  • Fewer wrong answers: fading AM is no longer taken for Morse or SSB; an off-tune voice or a heterodyne is no longer taken for PSK; fast or weak Morse is no longer taken for Hellschreiber.
    • 
      
  • The AUTO switch: pressed in while it's on, with a bar moving along its foot while it listens. Switching it off takes effect at once, even mid-listen.
    • 
    

    
Tuning and the keyboard

    
    
      
  • Clicking an SSB signal tunes to its carrier (just below the voice for USB, above it for LSB, with the usual sideband for the frequency) and then fine-tunes itself on the voice. In SSB, CW and the digital modes a click goes where you click, instead of stepping one channel.
    • 
      
  • Keyboard shortcuts: ↑ ↓ volume (Shift for fine), PgUp / PgDn next / previous band, A for AUTO, Space to pause the waterfall, Esc to close menus. Typing a number on the number row or the number pad starts a new frequency, from anywhere. The keyboard button next to ? (or K) shows them all.
    • 
      
  • Memory markers: each memory in view shows as a small tag (M1, M2…) at the foot of the spectrum: hover for what it is, click to recall it.
    • 
      
  • Changing band zooms back out to the full view; within a band the zoom stays.
    • 
    

    
Display

    
    
      
  • Clock under the frequency: UTC ("08:55Z"), the time schedules, fax charts, FT8 and logs use. Click it for local time.
    • 
      
  • Power-on lamp test: like a car's dashboard, pressing Power lights every light in the top bar for 2 seconds while the meter sweeps up and back.
    • 
      
  • Tidier top bar: wider zoom buttons with the Panels menu on its own row, the settings, keyboard and help buttons in one matching row, room for all the status lights, and status messages that follow band changes and memory recalls.
    • 
    

    
Decoders

    
    
      
  • FT4 (new): FT8's faster sibling, used for contests: decodes every 7.5 seconds, with the same list, clock correction and offline working as FT8. AUTO recognises it on its frequencies, and the demo has an FT4 station on 14.080 MHz.
    • 
      
  • FT8 and FT4 details: each decode now shows the station's country (from its callsign, using a table built into the app, so it works offline) and, with your location set in Settings → Decoders (pick your nearest city from 620 built in, type your locator, or let the computer say if it can), the distance (km and miles) and bearing. Hover over a line for more: continent, what the message is (CQ, report, RR73…), the grid. A bigger list in columns, an Expand button, a "CQ only" filter, sorting (click a column title: newest, farthest, strongest or by country), and calls to your callsign highlighted.
    • 
      
  • FT8 and FT4 listen 5 kHz wide instead of 3, for busy days when stations spill above the usual slice (6 kHz in 1.8, centred, for uncalibrated sticks).
    • 
      
  • PSK starts part-way through a transmission: tune into a QSO in progress and text appears within a couple of seconds, at any of the three speeds; it goes quiet as soon as the transmission ends.
    • 
      
  • Fixed: a decoder could stop for good after a single broken audio sample (most noticeably PSK, after changing modes several times). Broken samples are now filtered out before any decoder hears them, and PSK heals itself if one ever gets through.
    • 
      
  • RTTY sorts out mark and space by itself: it reads the signal both ways round and keeps whichever comes out as text, so no more gibberish until you press Reverse (which still works, by hand).
    • 
      
  • ACARS and FT8 stay on when you type another frequency that suits them. Choosing FT8 stays on the frequency you're on; choosing ACARS or FAX away from one of their stations goes to the top of their list (131.550 MHz; DWD Pinneberg, 3855 kHz).
    • 
    

    
Reliability

    
    
      
  • Switching off and on: two bugs fixed. The receiver could stop following the tuning after a restart (a tuner's tiny frequency rounding), and on a MacBook the tuner could miss its gain while waking up, leaving only noise. Both are put right automatically now.
    • 
      
  • The tuner's frequency lock is checked properly, and the frequency sent again if a lock fails.
    • 
      
  • Fewer false "samples lost" warnings while tuning around, and a clear message for sticks whose tuner chip can't be used (E4000, FC0012, FC0013, FC2580).
    • 
      
  • Diagnostics log: now also records the sound output, the signal level, each power on and off, and each OVL gain back-off step.
    • 
    

    
Other

    
    
      
  • Check for updates (top of this panel): looks on GitHub for a newer version, only when you click it. The project page link is just below it.
    • 
    

    
New in 1.6
    
    
      
  • Top bar: frequency, S-meter, mode, volume, mute, record, settings and help are always visible, on desktop and on phones.
    • 
      
  • One-click mode buttons: AUTO · FM · AM · SAM · USB · LSB · CW · More ▾. SAM-U, SAM-L, the decoders and Wide/Narrow FM are under More.
    • 
      
  • Settings dialog: receiver settings open from the gear icon, with tabs for Device, Display & tuning, Audio & recording, Decoders, Calibration and Backup.
    • 
      
  • No duplicate controls: mode, filter width and step each have one control.
    • 
      
  • Status lights under the frequency digits, and a larger S-meter reading that balances the frequency.
    • 
      
  • Layout stability: the Alerts button no longer shifts the spectrum toolbar, and the top bar no longer jumps in height on shortwave or when a frequency label appears.
    • 
      
  • Scrolling status line: a message too long for its space scrolls instead of being cut off (with "reduce motion" on, it's shortened and the whole message is on hover).
    • 
      
  • Seek / Step box pinned: it stays at the top of the side panel while the panels below scroll.
    • 
      
  • Panels menu in the Seek / Step box: jump straight to Band, Memories, Audio & gain and the rest. The zoom buttons are now −, + and the zoom level (click it for the full view).
    • 
      
  • Tall (portrait) view: on a Chromebook or tablet held upright, the page no longer scrolls, so the browser's tab and address bar stay put. The top bar, a slice of waterfall and the Seek / Step box stay in view, and only the panels below them scroll.
    • 
      
  • Fast band switching fixed: the spectrum and waterfall no longer freeze while the audio carries on. A band change made while the sample rate was still changing (entering or leaving the airband and 2 m sections, slower on a slow computer) is no longer lost. A watchdog also restarts the display if it stops, and resends the frequency if the stick and the display disagree, so you no longer need to go to another band and back.
    • 
      
  • USB stick recovery: unplugging the stick, or the stick resetting, no longer leaves the radio stuck. It goes back to Off cleanly, and if it was on, it starts again by itself when the stick is plugged back in. Clear messages for a lost stick, data stopping, samples going missing and the common USB errors (including the WinUSB driver on Windows).
    • 
      
  • Diagnostics log: Settings → Backup → Save diagnostics log saves the last three minutes of band changes, retunes and stick errors, to help track down a problem. No audio, memories or personal data.
    • 
      
  • OVL indicator next to the meter: amber when the band keeps touching full scale, red when the receiver is overloaded. Click it while it's lit and it lowers the RF gain step by step until the overload clears, then shows what it changed, with Undo.
    • 
      
  • RF gain per band: each band remembers its own RF gain, so a busy band can run lower without changing the others. (Automatic gain stays one setting for all bands.)
    • 
      
  • FT8 (More): decodes everyone in the passband every 15 seconds, and corrects the computer's clock from the stations it hears, so it works offline. The demo has FT8 stations on 14.074 MHz.
    • 
      
  • ACARS (More): aircraft text messages on the airband, decoded and listed. The demo has an ACARS station on 131.550 MHz.
    • 
      
  • PSK mode (was PSK31): decodes PSK31, PSK63 and PSK125, and finds the speed by itself. The demo has a PSK63 station on 7.0425 MHz (40 m).
    • 
      
  • Weather fax from any band: choosing FAX away from shortwave tunes to the first fax station in the list.
    • 
    

    

    
Keyboard shortcuts

    

    
Quick help

    
    
      
  • Works with the RTL-SDR Blog V4 (and V3), and the Nooelec NESDR SMArt v5, both tested by the OFFgrid-SDR author.
        Buy the Nooelec: Amazon UK · Amazon US.
    • 
      
  • Antennas tested with OFFgrid-SDR: the AURSINC GA800 active loop shortwave antenna (Amazon UK · Amazon US), and the YouLoop passive magnetic loop, which folds up small for travel (Amazon UK · Amazon US).
    • 
      
  • Zoom (under Seek and Step, or the + and − keys): Zoom + narrows the waterfall around the tuned signal, down to a few kHz across, with the detail to match, handy for SSB and CW. Default goes back to the full view.
    • 
      
  • Any frequency the stick can reach (100 kHz to 1766 MHz) can be typed into the frequency display. Add k or M to be explicit, e.g. 198k or 1090M; a plain number below 500 is MHz, 500 and above is kHz. Frequencies outside the bands open in General coverage, with a moving window and all modes (AM, SAM, USB, LSB, CW, NFM, WFM).
    • 
      
  • Panorama (next to the zoom buttons, green when on) sweeps the stick to show up to 10 MHz at once: Around me (centred where you're tuned, 2–10 MHz wide) or the HF slices 0.5–10, 10–20 and 20–28.8 MHz. The audio pauses while it sweeps. Click a signal to tune to it and listen, or click Panorama again to go back to where you were. Short bursts can be missed, since it looks at one slice at a time.
    • 
      
  • Replay (Receiver settings → Waterfall buffer: Off, 15, 30 or 60 s): keeps the last few seconds of the signal in memory. Press ⏸ (top left of the waterfall) to freeze it, draw a box around a signal, and a popout shows it in detail with Play (loops it), Save MP3 and Cancel. The replay window has its own mode, filter, SSB shift and noise filters, and in CW it decodes the Morse in just that section. Click in its picture to retune it; to loop just part of it press A/B and click the start and end (A/B again clears the loop); Save writes the audio (MP3) and the raw signal around the box (IQ WAV, for other SDR software). Space plays or pauses, Esc cancels; ▶ Live goes back to listening. Time marks down the left show how far back each row is; the dimmed part is older than the buffer, and dashed lines mark retunes (a box can't cross one). While paused, the mouse wheel over the waterfall scrolls back through the whole buffer (time marks move with it), and ⇕ Whole buffer squeezes all of it onto the screen; draw a box anywhere in it. An FM replay shows its own RDS (station name and RadioText). On phones and low-memory computers the longer buffers are greyed out, so the browser can't run short of memory.
    • 
      
  • CW tuning help: in CW, clicking near a signal on the waterfall tunes exactly onto it (the nearest carrier within ±400 Hz), so it sits on the tone. Z, or the Zero-beat button in the CW box, does the same for a signal within ±500 Hz of where you are.
    • 
      
  • AUTO (the first mode button, every band) is a switch: lit means on. While on, every time you tune somewhere new it listens for about 2 seconds, works out what the signal is, switches to that mode and tunes onto it, with a banner at the top of the waterfall (a progress bar while it listens, then what it found and how sure it is). It knows CW, RTTY, PSK31, NAVTEX, DSC, weather fax, SSTV, Hellschreiber, AM and SSB (sideband judged from the voice) on HF; narrowband FM and airband AM on VHF/UHF; wideband FM on the FM broadcast band. It also recognises DRM digital broadcasts (which can't be decoded here) and says so without changing anything. If nothing is clear it picks the band's usual mode: the ham band's sideband (LSB on 160/80/40 m, USB on 60 m and from 30 m up), AM on broadcast bands and the airband, narrowband FM elsewhere on VHF/UHF. Choose a mode yourself, or press AUTO again, to switch it off. On the airband, PMR446 and marine VHF it's instant, with no listening: they always use the same mode.
    • 
      
  • SSTV (More, any band but FM broadcast): slow-scan TV pictures, drawn bottom left as they arrive (Martin M1/M2, Scottie S1/S2, PD90/PD120, read from each picture's header). ◀ ▶ browse the last six; Save PNG keeps one at full size. USB on shortwave (14.230, 21.340, 28.680 MHz), LSB on 40 m and 80 m (7.171, 3.845 MHz), chosen by itself, FM on VHF (the ISS on 145.800 MHz).
    • 
      
  • DSC (More, below 30 MHz): ships' distress, urgency, safety and routine calls on the HF DSC frequencies (2187.5 to 16804.5 kHz), listed with who called whom (MMSI numbers); distress calls in red; unreadable digits as ??.
    • 
      
  • FT8 (More): the busiest digital mode on the ham bands. Tune to an FT8 frequency (14.074, 7.074, 3.573, 21.074, 28.074 MHz, USB) and every 15 seconds everyone in the passband is decoded at once and listed: UTC time, strength (dB), timing (DT, seconds), audio frequency (Hz) and message. CQ calls are highlighted. FT8 needs the clock right to within a second or so: without the internet the app sets it from the stations it hears (shown as "clock corrected"), so it works offline; a clock wrong by whole 15 s slots can't be detected, though. Choosing FT8 stays on the frequency you're on, so tune to an FT8 frequency first; typing another FT8 frequency while in FT8 keeps FT8 on.
    • 
      
  • HF upconverter (Ham It Up and others): Settings → Device. Auto sends MW, shortwave and HF (below 65 MHz) through the converter and everything above straight through, reminding you which way to set its switch; On uses it always. The frequency shown is always the real one.
    • 
      
  • Setup: Settings → Calibration → Run setup again goes through your location, the stick's calibration and the clock in one go, as on the first run. Clock details (there, or in the Time signal box) shows how far your computer's clock is out and how fast it drifts.
    • 
      
  • Time signal (More): sets the clock from the time stations CHU (3.330, 7.850, 14.670 MHz), WWV / WWVH (2.5 to 25 MHz) and RWM (4.996, 9.996, 14.996 MHz): the full time from CHU or WWV, the seconds from any station's ticks. FT8, FT4, WSPR and the clock at the top use it. Find a time station tries every frequency; Set by hand takes the time from a phone if none can be heard. (MSF and DCF77 are below the sticks' range.)
    • 
      
  • DRM (More): digital radio on long, medium and short wave, a flat block about 10 kHz wide. Tune to its centre (or let AUTO find it): the DRM box shows the station's name, language and audio type, the signal's settings, and plays the sound after about 5 seconds (DRM spreads each moment over up to 2 seconds so that it survives fading). AAC and xHE-AAC stations play, with SBR and parametric stereo. The station's text message shows under its details, and its SlideShow picture, if it sends one, top right (click for full size).
    • 
      
  • An SDRplay RSP, through SDRconnect: SDRplay's SDRconnect (1.0.6 or later; 1.0.10 still reports its API as 1.0.3) must already be running on the RSP's computer, with its WebSocket API on port 5454: on Linux or a Raspberry Pi, /opt/SDRconnect/SDRconnect_headless (it can be started at boot as a service: see SDRconnect.md, beside the README on GitHub); in SDRconnect's ordinary program, switch the WebSocket server on in its settings. Allow port 5454 through that computer's firewall. Then Settings → Device → SDRconnect, the address, Test, Power on; the NET badge shows the connection. An RSP1A or RSP1B needs nothing more; an RSPdx switches antennas by frequency (A from 30 MHz up, B below, by default, changeable in Settings → Device once it's running); an RSPduo uses one tuner. No bias-tee control (use the antenna's own injector) and no Panorama through SDRconnect. The RF gain slider sets the RSP's front-end (LNA) gain, with full gain only in its last tenth (it overloads easily); the IF gain is left to SDRconnect's AGC; Auto picks the middle setting for each band. On a 1 GB Pi, use Raspberry Pi OS Lite: with a desktop it runs short of memory and DAB cuts out.
    • 

  • VDL2 (More → Aircraft): aircraft datalink at 136.6–137 MHz, every channel in view decoded at once; the bursts are short and often too weak to see on the waterfall, but they're decoded. The buttons along the top filter by channel; "Messages only" hides acknowledgements.
    • 
      
  • DAB (the DAB tab): digital radio on VHF, 174–240 MHz. Choose a channel (5A to 13F), or tune anywhere in a multiplex with AUTO on. The DAB box lists the multiplex's stations: click one to listen (DAB+ and the original DAB, at any bit rate). It shows each station's format, programme type and "now playing" text, and its logo or SlideShow picture top right, where the multiplex sends one: hover over the multiplex's name to see which.
    • 
      
  • AIS (More): ships' names, positions, courses and destinations, on both marine channels at once. Each vessel shows once, updated as it's heard, with its distance and bearing; hover for its details (MMSI, flag, call sign, size, ETA). Works best near the coast or a big river, with the antenna up high.
    • 
      
  • APRS (More): radio amateurs' positions (cars, walkers, balloons), weather stations, messages and status reports, sent as short data bursts on one VHF frequency per region (144.800 MHz in Europe). Choosing APRS goes to the one for your location; the list in the box has the others. Each station shows with its distance and bearing, speed and heading, and weather in metric units; hover for its exact position and the digipeaters it came through.
    • 
      
  • WSPR (More): weak beacons from radio amateurs (callsign, locator, power), sent in 2-minute slots on fixed frequencies and decoded far below what you can hear (to about -28 dB). They show in the FT8 list with country, distance and power; a band list is at the top of the box. Choosing WSPR goes to 20 m (14.0956 MHz) unless you're on a WSPR frequency. If the stations land away from 1500 Hz, the box shows how far off the stick is and offers to Correct it. WSPR finds its stations even with the clock a minute or so out, and their timing then corrects the clock.
    • 
      
  • FT4 (More): FT8's faster sibling, used for contests and quick contacts (7.0475, 14.080, 21.140, 3.575 MHz, USB). Every 7.5 seconds it decodes everyone in the passband and lists them like FT8, sharing FT8's clock correction. Choosing FT4 stays on the frequency you're on.
    • 
      
  • ACARS (More, airband): short text messages between aircraft and the ground, listed bottom left with the time, aircraft registration, flight and label. Try 131.550, 131.525, 131.725 or 136.900 MHz; messages come in short bursts. Only messages that pass their checksum are shown, so there's no garbage. Choosing ACARS when you're not on an ACARS channel tunes to 131.550 MHz, the first in the list; typing another airband frequency while in ACARS keeps ACARS on. (Messages only: nothing is plotted. Listening rules for aircraft messages differ by country.)
    • 
      
  • PSK (More, below 30 MHz): keyboard-to-keyboard ham text (around 14.070, 7.040, 3.580 MHz). It decodes PSK31, PSK63 and PSK125, finds the speed by itself and shows it in the PSK box, and starts within a couple of seconds even part-way through a transmission. Click on a signal to snap onto it; the decoder then follows it.
    • 
      
  • Hellschreiber (More, below 30 MHz): the tone paints the letters on a strip bottom left, shown twice stacked so there's always a complete row to read.
    • 
      
  • NAVTEX (More, below 30 MHz): maritime safety and weather messages on 518 kHz (English), 490 kHz and 4209.5 kHz, decoded bottom left with each message's header (station, subject, number). Each character is sent twice, so damaged ones are repaired from the second copy.
    • 
      
  • RTTY (More, shortwave): radioteletype from weather and news stations and radio amateurs, decoded to text bottom left. It finds the two tones (170, 425, 450 or 850 Hz apart) and the speed (45.45, 50 or 75 baud) itself, so tune near the signal. If the text is gibberish, press Reverse.
    • 
      
  • RDS status: on FM the RDS box is always shown, with a line saying searching, no data (often a signal too weak for RDS, even if the audio is fine) or locked with the share of RDS data received cleanly.
    • 
      
  • Frequency calibration (Receiver settings): pick a time station (RWM, WWV, CHU…) and press Calibrate. It tunes there, measures the carrier to a fraction of a hertz and sets the frequency correction (ppm). Best after the stick has warmed up for 10–15 minutes.
    • 
      
  • Low-power mode (top of Receiver settings): for older or slower computers. It halves the samples the stick sends and draws the display half as often; an LP light shows while it's on. If the computer struggles (audio gaps, a very slow display, or high CPU for half a minute) OFFgrid-SDR suggests it; it never switches it on by itself.
    • 
      
  • AGC speed (Audio & gain, in SSB and CW): how quickly the volume recovers after a loud moment. Slow suits SSB voice; Fast suits CW and fast-changing signals.
    • 
      
  • Peak · Avg · Alerts (above the spectrum): Peak holds a faint line at the strongest level each frequency has reached recently; Avg smooths the spectrum so weak steady signals stand out; Alerts flashes a ring where a signal appears on a frequency that has been empty for two minutes (fading stations don't count). Each is off by default and pauses in Low-power mode.
    • 
      
  • Labels: right-click on the spectrum or waterfall to add a label at that frequency (e.g. "Local repeater"); right-click an existing one to edit or remove it. Labels show on the spectrum and under the frequency, and are saved in settings backups.
    • 
      
  • Logbook (side panel): date and time (UTC), frequency, mode, signal (average and peak S/N), station and notes. Stations you stay on for 30 s with a signal, and decoder results (NAVTEX, DSC, SSTV, fax), are logged by themselves; Log now adds one any time. The station is filled in where OFFgrid-SDR knows it (your labels, RDS, the built-in lists, decoders, callsigns heard in CW, RTTY or PSK31). Click Station or Notes to edit; ✕ deletes. Export CSV saves it for a spreadsheet; Save to a file keeps one file up to date (Chrome and Edge on a computer); or tick "Automatically create a CSV log file".
    • 
      
  • Start: press Power on, pick your stick in the USB chooser, then choose a band.
    • 
      
  • Type a frequency: click the big frequency display (or just type digits) and press Enter. 98.8 → FM, 909 → MW, 6070 or 6.07 → the whole 49 m band.
    • 
      
  • Waterfall: click a signal to tune to it, or click anywhere else to tune there. Clicking close to the tuning line steps one channel left or right, for fine nudging. Shift-click tunes to the exact spot. In band views you can tune anywhere visible, including just outside the official band edges. Arrow keys and the mouse wheel stop at the edge of the view.
    • 
      
  • Seek stops on the first channel above the squelch level (dB of S/N).
    • 
      
  • Mode buttons (top bar): the same eight on every band. AUTO · FM · AM · SAM · USB · LSB · CW · More ▾. FM is wideband on the FM broadcast band and narrowband elsewhere (repeaters, PMR, marine). SAM is synchronous AM (stops fading distortion); SAM-U / SAM-L use one sideband only, to dodge a neighbour splattering into the other side. USB / LSB for SSB (100 Hz steps); CW for Morse (a 600 Hz tone, 100 to 1000 Hz filter on the badge, 10 Hz steps). More ▾ holds SAM-U and SAM-L, the decoders (RTTY, PSK, FT8, FT4, NAVTEX, ACARS, DSC, weather fax, SSTV, Hellschreiber) and the explicit FM types, Wide FM and Narrow FM. Modes that don't fit where you're tuned are greyed, with the reason in the tooltip (e.g. AM on the FM broadcast band). On wideband FM, Stereo · Wide · Mono appear next to the step button. On a phone the mode buttons fold into a single mode menu.
    • 
      
  • Meter: click the scale button to switch between dBFS, S-meter and S/N. Calibrate the S-meter in Receiver settings.
    • 
      
  • OVL (next to the meter) watches the whole band the stick receives, not just the tuned channel. Amber: the band keeps touching full scale; overload is only a dB or two away (a single click or crash doesn't count). Red: the receiver is overloaded: strong stations are clipping all the time and mixing with each other, which fills the band with false signals on every channel. Click OVL while it's lit to lower the RF gain until it clears (Undo puts it back), or turn on automatic gain. Each band keeps its own RF gain.
    • 
      
  • Broadcast / Ham / Mystery under the band tabs (on SW) switches the grid between the shortwave broadcast metre bands and the amateur bands (160 to 10 m, plus 2 m on VHF, which runs the stick at 2.4 MS/s so the whole 144–146 MHz band fits on the waterfall, and 70 cm on UHF, 430–440 MHz, which is too wide for one view and tunes with a moving window). PMR446 (in the Ham tab) is the licence-free walkie-talkie band used in the UK and Europe: 16 NFM channels from 446.00625 to 446.19375 MHz, all shown at once. Step + / Step − and the mouse wheel move channel by channel, and the readout and banner show the channel number. Mystery collects famous unexplained HF stations: The Buzzer (UVB-76), The Pip, The Squeaky Wheel and other Russian military "channel markers". Each opens a narrow view on the station; they're mostly buzzes and beeps, with rare voice messages. Air (its own tab) covers the airband, 118–137 MHz, in 2 MHz sections, each shown whole, in AM with 8.33 kHz channel steps (25 kHz on the step badge). The display shows 8.33 kHz channel names, and typing one (e.g. 118.510) tunes that channel. Squelch (the SQ light) is handy there, as most channels are silent between calls. Each ham band always opens in its own mode (LSB below 10 MHz, USB above, 60 m USB, FM on 2 m, 70 cm and PMR446) and remembers its last frequency and step; a broadcast band remembers whether you use AM or SAM. A mode AUTO picks is for that signal only.
    • 
      
  • Signal info popup: switch it on in Receiver settings. Hover over a signal to see its frequency, level, height above the noise and width, plus the band plan and any label you gave it. Zoom in for more accurate widths. Off by default.
    • 
      
  • Demo mode: open the page as index.html?demo to try everything without a stick. The Demo stations list tunes simulated stations: four FM stations (stereo and RDS), the 49 m band with a station for each filter (fading for SAM, mains hum, hum plus a whistle for Find whine, a station a little off its channel for AUTO, electric-fence clicks for the noise blanker, and a weak hissy station for noise reduction), and the 41 m band with SSB voice in LSB and USB, a CW Morse beacon and an AM broadcaster. SSTV is also sent in LSB on 7.171 MHz.
    • 
      
  • Scan (Memories, next to Store and Clear): press Scan and your stored memories pulse gold. Tap the ones you want to scan: each turns green and the scan starts, hopping from one to the next and stopping on any whose signal reaches the Squelch setting (in dB over the noise), then carrying on 3 seconds after the signal ends. Set the Squelch first: with it Open the scan can't tell signals from noise and stays on the first memory. Tap a green memory to take it out of the scan. While it hops the stick runs at its lowest sample rate and the waterfall is paused (the spectrum stays); the waterfall comes back while it is stopped on a signal. Press Scan again to stop and stay where you are. Tuning by hand, Seek, Store or Clear also stops the scan.
    • 
      
  • Identify ↗ (above the waterfall, when online): opens a new tab: a web search for "what is on" the frequency you're tuned to, a question to Google's AI Mode, or (below 30 MHz) the shortwave radio schedule for that frequency on shortwave.live. Both send the frequency (and, for the AI, the mode and the UTC time) to that site, only when you click. AI answers can be wrong, so check them against the web results or a schedule.
    • 
      
  • CW decoder: in CW mode, Morse is turned into text in a box at the bottom left, with the speed in WPM. It learns the sender's speed by itself and stays blank on noise. It works best on clean, steady signals such as beacons (switch it off in Receiver settings).
    • 
      
  • Settings backup (Receiver settings): Export saves all memories and settings to a small file, for example to keep on the USB stick; Import restores them, on this or another computer.
    • 
      
  • FAX (weather fax, shortwave): choose a station from the list in the fax box, or tune a listed frequency and pick FAX mode. Charts are sent at scheduled times: the decoder waits for each chart's start tone, lines it up automatically and builds the picture line by line (about 10 minutes per chart at 120 lines a minute). "Start now" begins mid-chart; then click the chart where its left edge should be. Save PNG keeps the full-resolution chart.
    • 
      
  • SSB filter: in USB or LSB, click the filter badge (under the mode buttons, in the top bar) for 1.8, 2, 2.4 or 2.8 kHz. Passband shift (Audio & gain) slides the filter up or down without changing the pitch, to dodge a station just above or below. Both are remembered per band and in memories. Auto notch (the Notch button under Audio & gain, green when on) removes steady whistles from AM and SSB within about a second; it may also remove long held musical notes, so leave it off for music.
    • 
      
  • RDS on FM: the station name, RadioText, programme type and clock appear in a box at the bottom left of the waterfall once they're decoded. FM memories and recordings pick up the station name.
    • 
      
  • REC (or R) records what you hear. Press again to stop, and the recording downloads as MP3 (or WAV, in Receiver settings).
    • 
      
  • Noise filters (MW/SW, Audio & gain): Reduction for hiss; Hum 50/60 Hz for mains buzz; AI voice (Off, Light, Med, Strong, Full), a small neural network that clears hiss, roar and noise-type jamming from speech (the stronger settings quieten music, and Full silences it); Blanker for clicks and pops; Whistles, an automatic notch for steady whistles; and Whine, the smart notch: it finds a steady whine (skipping mains hum: that's the Hum button's job) and notches it at once. Its strip below shows the audio: click it to drop a notch where you like, drag a notch's line until the whine disappears, scroll over it to nudge it, right-click it to remove it. A long held musical note can look like a whine. Notches clear when you change station.
    • 
      
  • Equaliser and audio extensions (such as Equalizer Plus) work with OFFgrid-SDR like any other page. If you open it as a file (the address starts file:///), Chrome needs you to allow each extension first: go to chrome://extensions, click Details on the extension, and turn on Allow access to file URLs, then reload OFFgrid-SDR.
    • 
      
  • Keys: ← → step, Shift + ← → seek, M mute, ? this panel.
    •
